title: Breaking And Entering: Julia Jacklin and RVG on their cover of Bjork's "Army of Me"
summary: Host Simon Winkler talks to Julia Jacklin and Romy Vager from Melbourne's RVG, about their new collaborative cover of Bjork's legendary track "Army of Me".
transcript:
Julia Jacklin and Romy Vager of RVG joined Simon Winkler via Zoom on Breaking and Entering on 27 May 2021 to discuss their collaborative cover of Björk's 'Army of Me' for the RISING Singles Club. Edited for length and clarity.

Simon: I'm very sorry that, with the current developments, the shows that were going to take place this weekend as part of RISING can't happen. Julia, your second album, Crushing, came out in 2019 and was an Album of the Week here. You've both been busy with performances: Romy, as part of Our Golden Friend's birthday celebrations earlier this year, and Julia, with a number of sold-out shows at the end of last year. Hopefully we'll get to see you both on stage very soon. The RISING Singles Club produces a cover by a beloved artist to coincide with every full moon. Did you both get to see last night's supermoon lunar eclipse?

Julia: I had binoculars, so I got a pretty zoomed-in look. It was very nice.

Romy: I saw it behind some clouds, but a friend showed me some nice pictures that a housemate took of it, so I feel like I've seen it.

Simon: 'Army of Me' is the Björk song you've selected to cover. Julia, you said you were listening to it over and over on a treadmill to make you feel stronger than you are. Could you tell us more about your personal relationship with this track?

Julia: I grew up listening to Björk. She was my dad's favourite artist. I felt like we didn't have heaps to talk about growing up, but we could connect over music. In terms of this collaboration, I can't say I put too much thought into it. I was just listening to it a lot while I was running, because I was trying to become someone who runs regularly. I feel like I need to listen to music that makes me feel like I'm preparing for battle in order to exercise. So I was listening to this song a lot, and then I had to do this song for RISING, and I wanted to do it with someone. RVG is my favourite band basically of all time. So I was like, I'm going to reach out and see if they want to try and mesh our two quite different styles together over this song.

Romy: It's a dream. We were like, yeah.

Simon: Romy, are there particular songs, playlists, artists or albums you've been turning to in recent times for strength or motivation?

Romy: I got really into Slayer last year because I needed to refresh my batteries a bit. As a joke to myself, I went, 'I'm just going to start listening to Slayer.' Then I just got really into it. I went the opposite way. I liked listening to things that were completely left field for me, things that I would never approach. That's been my angle.

Simon: It's funny you should say that, because I was reading that 'Army of Me' has been covered a number of times. Björk put together a fundraising covers and remixes album, and apparently it's a song that a lot of metal and nu metal bands have covered. Was this a chance for both of you to lean into that side of your musical selves?

Julia: I feel like the whole time we were recording this song, we kept looking at each other with raised eyebrows, being like, is this good? For me, probably more because I was coming in just singing, it felt quite out of my comfort zone, but in a very good way. I think it's good, though. We came to that conclusion, didn't we, Romy?

Romy: Yeah, we definitely did.

Julia: When you do stuff out of your comfort zone, you're always a bit like, am I going crazy? I feel like I just needed one person in the room to be like, no, it's good. But I think we were all just like, I think so.

Romy: Speaking from RVG, we don't give a lot of compliments. We're a bit cold sometimes.

Simon: Romy, you said you saw this collaboration as an opportunity to challenge yourselves and do things you hadn't done before while having fun. What were some of the challenges or surprises during the recording process?

Romy: Reuben bought a keyboard synthesiser, I think during lockdown last year. This was a good way to branch out a bit and do some freaky sounds, really.

Simon: Julia, you mentioned that coming in purely to use your voice was unfamiliar. Is that right?

Julia: Yeah. I have a tendency to think that I'm pretty terrible a lot of the time, and I think a lot of musicians do. I really question my own abilities a lot. Going into a room with a whole new group of musicians can be really terrifying, because in those moments you have to draw upon all your knowledge and be able to communicate it well. That was quite challenging, but it was such a nice day of recording. After not being in a studio for a couple of years, being in a room where everyone was so willing to try stuff out ended up being such a supportive, lovely experience. I think we all left feeling inspired to make new stuff. Even though we didn't write the song, a lot of our job is to explore and to try new things. Sometimes you can stop doing that because it's a bit too scary, because it might sound terrible and you'll embarrass yourself. But I definitely walked away from it being like, oh, I can do this. I can express my ideas and I can work with new people. It was really great.

Simon: Björk mentioned that 'Army of Me' was partly written as encouragement to her younger brother, who she saw struggling to get motivated, and that he's symbolically represented in the video. It made me think of songs as gifts to the world, but also to close friends or family. Julia, I heard you talking to Zan Rowe about family as a focus of songwriting. You've described 'Comfort', from your last album, as a song you would send to friends who might need it. Could you tell us about the songs you've been working on that explore family dynamics?

Julia: Like my songs?

Simon: Yeah.

Julia: Apparently, 'Army of Me' was written by Björk about her younger brother. I think it sounds kind of mean.

Simon: It's pretty direct, I guess.

Julia: She's not being super kind. It really reminds me, because I have a younger brother who I don't think will be listening. I could resonate a lot with that frustration of a younger sibling who you don't feel has got things together. I really liked that, especially because if you listen to the song for the first time, you would probably think it's about big, grand ideas or self-empowerment. But it comes down to her being frustrated with her little brother, which I love. I lived with my family for a lot of last year, which I hadn't done in over ten years, and I've been writing quite a lot of stuff about them, which I think is the hardest topic to write about. They're the most difficult relationships to navigate a lot of the time. I do want to write more about it, but I find it very challenging because it feels way more personal than a love song or a heartbreak. It feels almost illegal. We shouldn't be saying these things about our own parents or something. I don't know.

Simon: Romy, empathy is at the heart of your writing too. After the album release, you've been focused on performances, including a show in Sydney later this year for Vivid. In the midst of everything, have you been writing as well?

Romy: Yeah, it's been really good. We've slowly been introducing new songs to the set, which is the first time we've done that in a while this year. It was really good to refresh my batteries. I'm trying to write new things, figure out stuff that I haven't said before and challenge myself, I guess.

Simon: Thank you both for joining us, and for the incredible new song. We can't wait to see you playing again, hopefully very soon.
aliases: Julia Jacklin and RVG on their cover of Bjork's "Army of Me"
